lemma to_partrec' {n} {f : List.Vector ℕ n →. ℕ} (hf : ArithPart₁ f) : Partrec' f := by
  induction hf
  case zero => exact Partrec'.of_part (Partrec.const' 0)
  case one  => exact Partrec'.of_part (Partrec.const' 1)
  case add n i j =>
    exact (Partrec'.of_part ((Primrec.nat_add.comp
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j))).to_comp.partrec))
  case mul n i j =>
    exact (Partrec'.of_part ((Primrec.nat_mul.comp
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j))).to_comp.partrec))
  case proj n i =>
    exact Partrec'.of_part
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i)).to_comp.partrec
  case equal n i j =>
    have : Primrec (fun (v : List.Vector ℕ n) => if v.get i = v.get j then 1 else 0) :=
      Primrec.ite
        (Primrec.eq.comp
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j)))
        (_root_.Primrec.const 1)
        (_root_.Primrec.const 0)
    exact Partrec'.of_part this.to_comp.partrec
  case lt n i j =>
    have : Primrec (fun (v : List.Vector ℕ n) => if v.get i < v.get j then 1 else 0) :=
      Primrec.ite
        (Primrec.nat_lt.comp
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j)))
        (_root_.Primrec.const 1)
        (_root_.Primrec.const 0)
    exact Partrec'.of_part this.to_comp.partrec
  case comp m n f g _ _ hf hg =>
    exact Partrec'.comp g hf hg
  case rfind f _ hf =>
    exact Partrec'.rfind hf

  | proj {n} (i : Fin n) : @ArithPart₁ n (fun v => v.get i : List.Vector ℕ n → ℕ)

lemma to_partrec' {n} {f : List.Vector ℕ n →. ℕ} (hf : ArithPart₁ f) : Partrec' f := by
  induction hf
  case zero => exact Partrec'.of_part (Partrec.const' 0)
  case one  => exact Partrec'.of_part (Partrec.const' 1)
  case add n i j =>
    exact (Partrec'.of_part ((Primrec.nat_add.comp
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j))).to_comp.partrec))
  case mul n i j =>
    exact (Partrec'.of_part ((Primrec.nat_mul.comp
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j))).to_comp.partrec))
  case proj n i =>
    exact Partrec'.of_part
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i)).to_comp.partrec
  case equal n i j =>
    have : Primrec (fun (v : List.Vector ℕ n) => if v.get i = v.get j then 1 else 0) :=
      Primrec.ite
        (Primrec.eq.comp
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j)))
        (_root_.Primrec.const 1)
        (_root_.Primrec.const 0)
    exact Partrec'.of_part this.to_comp.partrec
  case lt n i j =>
    have : Primrec (fun (v : List.Vector ℕ n) => if v.get i < v.get j then 1 else 0) :=
      Primrec.ite
        (Primrec.nat_lt.comp
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j)))
        (_root_.Primrec.const 1)
        (_root_.Primrec.const 0)
    exact Partrec'.of_part this.to_comp.partrec
  case comp m n f g _ _ hf hg =>
    exact Partrec'.comp g hf hg
  case rfind f _ hf =>
    exact Partrec'.rfind hf

lemma to_partrec' {n} {f : List.Vector ℕ n →. ℕ} (hf : ArithPart₁ f) : Partrec' f := by
  induction hf
  case zero => exact Partrec'.of_part (Partrec.const' 0)
  case one  => exact Partrec'.of_part (Partrec.const' 1)
  case add n i j =>
    exact (Partrec'.of_part ((Primrec.nat_add.comp
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j))).to_comp.partrec))
  case mul n i j =>
    exact (Partrec'.of_part ((Primrec.nat_mul.comp
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j))).to_comp.partrec))
  case proj n i =>
    exact Partrec'.of_part
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i)).to_comp.partrec
  case equal n i j =>
    have : Primrec (fun (v : List.Vector ℕ n) => if v.get i = v.get j then 1 else 0) :=
      Primrec.ite
        (Primrec.eq.comp
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j)))
        (_root_.Primrec.const 1)
        (_root_.Primrec.const 0)
    exact Partrec'.of_part this.to_comp.partrec
  case lt n i j =>
    have : Primrec (fun (v : List.Vector ℕ n) => if v.get i < v.get j then 1 else 0) :=
      Primrec.ite
        (Primrec.nat_lt.comp
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j)))
        (_root_.Primrec.const 1)
        (_root_.Primrec.const 0)
    exact Partrec'.of_part this.to_comp.partrec
  case comp m n f g _ _ hf hg =>
    exact Partrec'.comp g hf hg
  case rfind f _ hf =>
    exact Partrec'.rfind hf

lemma bind (f : List.Vector ℕ n → ℕ →. ℕ) (hf : @ArithPart₁ (n + 1) fun v => f v.tail v.head) {g} (hg : @ArithPart₁ n g) :
    @ArithPart₁ n fun v => (g v).bind (f v) :=
  (hf.comp (g :> fun i v => v.get i) (fun i => by cases i using Fin.cases <;> simp[*]; exact proj _)).of_eq (by
    intro v; simp
    rcases Part.eq_none_or_eq_some (g v) with (hgv | ⟨x, hgv⟩)
    · simp[hgv, List.Vector.mOfFn]
    · simp[hgv, Matrix.comp_vecCons']
      have : List.Vector.mOfFn (fun i => (g :> fun j v => Part.some $ v.get j) i v) = pure (List.Vector.ofFn (x :> fun j => v.get j)) := by
        rw[←List.Vector.mOfFn_pure]; apply congr_arg
        funext i; cases i using Fin.cases <;> simp[hgv]
      simp[this])

open Mathlib List.Vector Part Nat.Primrec
informal_statement: For any function \( f \) that takes two elements and a structure \( ![g, h] \) that holds two functions \( g \) and \( h \), applying \( f \) to the outputs of \( g \) and \( h \) is equivalent to first applying \( f \) to the pair \( ![g, h] \) and then interpreting it.
informal_proof:
To understand this, let's break it down. Suppose we have two functions \( g \) and \( h \), and another function \( f \) that takes two elements. The structure \( ![g, h] \) presumably contains these two functions. 

When we apply \( f \) to \( g \) and \( h \) individually, we get \( f(g(v), h(v)) \) for some value \( v \). On the other hand, applying \( f \) to the structure \( ![g, h] \) would also give \( f(g(v), h(v)) \). Since both operations result in the same value, they are equivalent.

This equivalence holds because both methods ultimately rely on applying \( f \) to the outcomes of \( g \) and \( h \), without any additional transformations beyond what's necessary for interpretation.

lemma to_partrec' {n} {f : List.Vector ℕ n →. ℕ} (hf : ArithPart₁ f) : Partrec' f := by
  induction hf
  case zero => exact Partrec'.of_part (Partrec.const' 0)
  case one  => exact Partrec'.of_part (Partrec.const' 1)
  case add n i j =>
    exact (Partrec'.of_part ((Primrec.nat_add.comp
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j))).to_comp.partrec))
  case mul n i j =>
    exact (Partrec'.of_part ((Primrec.nat_mul.comp
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j))).to_comp.partrec))
  case proj n i =>
    exact Partrec'.of_part
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i)).to_comp.partrec
  case equal n i j =>
    have : Primrec (fun (v : List.Vector ℕ n) => if v.get i = v.get j then 1 else 0) :=
      Primrec.ite
        (Primrec.eq.comp
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j)))
        (_root_.Primrec.const 1)
        (_root_.Primrec.const 0)
    exact Partrec'.of_part this.to_comp.partrec
  case lt n i j =>
    have : Primrec (fun (v : List.Vector ℕ n) => if v.get i < v.get j then 1 else 0) :=
      Primrec.ite
        (Primrec.nat_lt.comp
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j)))
        (_root_.Primrec.const 1)
        (_root_.Primrec.const 0)
    exact Partrec'.of_part this.to_comp.partrec
  case comp m n f g _ _ hf hg =>
    exact Partrec'.comp g hf hg
  case rfind f _ hf =>
    exact Partrec'.rfind hf

/--
**Function extensionality** is the statement that if two functions take equal values
every point, then the functions themselves are equal: `(∀ x, f x = g x) → f = g`.
It is called "extensionality" because it talks about how to prove two objects are equal
based on the properties of the object (compare with set extensionality,
which is `(∀ x, x ∈ s ↔ x ∈ t) → s = t`).

This is often an axiom in dependent type theory systems, because it cannot be proved
from the core logic alone. However in lean's type theory this follows from the existence
of quotient types (note the `Quot.sound` in the proof, as well as the `show` line
which makes use of the definitional equality `Quot.lift f h (Quot.mk x) = f x`).
-/
theorem funext {α : Sort u} {β : α → Sort v} {f g : (x : α) → β x}
    (h : ∀ x, f x = g x) : f = g := by
  let eqv (f g : (x : α) → β x) := ∀ x, f x = g x
  let extfunApp (f : Quot eqv) (x : α) : β x :=
    Quot.liftOn f
      (fun (f : ∀ (x : α), β x) => f x)
      (fun _ _ h => h x)
  show extfunApp (Quot.mk eqv f) = extfunApp (Quot.mk eqv g)
  exact congrArg extfunApp (Quot.sound h)

C1_dependencies.name: List.Vector
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`List.Vector α n` is the type of lists of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Note that there is also `Vector α n` in the root namespace,
which is the type of *arrays* of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Typically, if you are doing programming or verification, you will primarily use `Vector α n`,
and if you are doing mathematics, you may want to use `List.Vector α n` instead.
-/
def List.Vector (α : Type u) (n : ℕ) :=
  { l : List α // l.length = n }

lemma to_partrec' {n} {f : List.Vector ℕ n →. ℕ} (hf : ArithPart₁ f) : Partrec' f := by
  induction hf
  case zero => exact Partrec'.of_part (Partrec.const' 0)
  case one  => exact Partrec'.of_part (Partrec.const' 1)
  case add n i j =>
    exact (Partrec'.of_part ((Primrec.nat_add.comp
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j))).to_comp.partrec))
  case mul n i j =>
    exact (Partrec'.of_part ((Primrec.nat_mul.comp
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j))).to_comp.partrec))
  case proj n i =>
    exact Partrec'.of_part
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i)).to_comp.partrec
  case equal n i j =>
    have : Primrec (fun (v : List.Vector ℕ n) => if v.get i = v.get j then 1 else 0) :=
      Primrec.ite
        (Primrec.eq.comp
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j)))
        (_root_.Primrec.const 1)
        (_root_.Primrec.const 0)
    exact Partrec'.of_part this.to_comp.partrec
  case lt n i j =>
    have : Primrec (fun (v : List.Vector ℕ n) => if v.get i < v.get j then 1 else 0) :=
      Primrec.ite
        (Primrec.nat_lt.comp
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j)))
        (_root_.Primrec.const 1)
        (_root_.Primrec.const 0)
    exact Partrec'.of_part this.to_comp.partrec
  case comp m n f g _ _ hf hg =>
    exact Partrec'.comp g hf hg
  case rfind f _ hf =>
    exact Partrec'.rfind hf

lemma pos_of_eq_one (h : n = 1) : 0 < n := by simp[h]

def isEqNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n = m then 1 else 0

def isLtNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n < m then 1 else 0

def isLeNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ≤ m then 1 else 0

def isDvdNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ∣ m then 1 else 0

@[simp] lemma isEqNat_pos_iff : 0 < isEqNat n m ↔ n = m := by simp[isEqNat]; by_cases n = m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLtNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLtNat n m ↔ n < m := by simp[isLtNat]; by_cases n < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLeNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLeNat n m ↔ n ≤ m := by simp[isLeNat]; by_cases n ≤ m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isDvdNat_pos_iff : 0 < isDvdNat n m ↔ n ∣ m := by simp[isDvdNat]; by_cases n ∣ m <;> simp[*]

def inv (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isEqNat n 0

def pos (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 n

@[simp] lemma inv_zero : inv 0 = 1 := rfl

@[simp] lemma inv_iff_ne_zero : inv n = 0 ↔ 0 < n := by simp[inv, isEqNat, zero_lt_iff]

@[simp] lemma inv_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : inv n = 0 := by simp[inv, isEqNat, h]

@[simp] lemma pos_zero : pos 0 = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma pos_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : pos n = 1 := by simp[pos, isLtNat, h]

lemma to_partrec' {n} {f : List.Vector ℕ n →. ℕ} (hf : ArithPart₁ f) : Partrec' f := by

  case one  => exact Partrec'.of_part (Partrec.const' 1)
  case add n i j =>
    exact (Partrec'.of_part ((Primrec.nat_add.comp
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j))).to_comp.partrec))
  case mul n i j =>
    exact (Partrec'.of_part ((Primrec.nat_mul.comp
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j))).to_comp.partrec))
  case proj n i =>
    exact Partrec'.of_part
      (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i)).to_comp.partrec
  case equal n i j =>
    have : Primrec (fun (v : List.Vector ℕ n) => if v.get i = v.get j then 1 else 0) :=
      Primrec.ite
        (Primrec.eq.comp
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j)))
        (_root_.Primrec.const 1)
        (_root_.Primrec.const 0)
    exact Partrec'.of_part this.to_comp.partrec
  case lt n i j =>
    have : Primrec (fun (v : List.Vector ℕ n) => if v.get i < v.get j then 1 else 0) :=
      Primrec.ite
        (Primrec.nat_lt.comp
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const i))
          (Primrec.vector_get.comp _root_.Primrec.id (_root_.Primrec.const j)))
        (_root_.Primrec.const 1)
        (_root_.Primrec.const 0)
    exact Partrec'.of_part this.to_comp.partrec
  case comp m n f g _ _ hf hg =>
    exact Partrec'.comp g hf hg
  case rfind f _ hf =>
    exact Partrec'.rfind hf

informal_statement: The lemma asserts that the composition of arithmetic parts `f` and `g` satisfies the equality `(f ∘ g) _ _ = g _ ∘ f _`.
informal_proof:
To prove the statement, we consider the definition of function composition and analyze the behavior of the arithmetic parts `f` and `g`.

1. **Case 1: `g v` is `none`**  
   - If `g v` is `none`, then by the properties of composition and `mOfFn`, the composition `f ∘ g` directly yields the same result as `g ∘ f`.
   - This ensures that both sides of the equation align when there is no value present.

2. **Case 2: `g v` is `some x`**  
   - When `g v` is `some x`, the composition must be explicitly constructed.
   - By defining the result as `pure (List.Vector.ofFn (x :> fun j => v.get j))`, we ensure consistency in the composition.
   - This step verifies that the composition maintains the expected behavior even when values are explicitly present.

By exhaustively checking both cases, we confirm that the composition `(f ∘ g) _ _` equals `g _ ∘ f _`, thus proving the lemma.

lemma pos_of_eq_one (h : n = 1) : 0 < n := by simp[h]

def isEqNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n = m then 1 else 0

def isLtNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n < m then 1 else 0

def isLeNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ≤ m then 1 else 0

def isDvdNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ∣ m then 1 else 0

@[simp] lemma isEqNat_pos_iff : 0 < isEqNat n m ↔ n = m := by simp[isEqNat]; by_cases n = m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLtNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLtNat n m ↔ n < m := by simp[isLtNat]; by_cases n < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLeNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLeNat n m ↔ n ≤ m := by simp[isLeNat]; by_cases n ≤ m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isDvdNat_pos_iff : 0 < isDvdNat n m ↔ n ∣ m := by simp[isDvdNat]; by_cases n ∣ m <;> simp[*]

def inv (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isEqNat n 0

def pos (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 n

@[simp] lemma inv_zero : inv 0 = 1 := rfl

@[simp] lemma inv_iff_ne_zero : inv n = 0 ↔ 0 < n := by simp[inv, isEqNat, zero_lt_iff]

@[simp] lemma inv_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : inv n = 0 := by simp[inv, isEqNat, h]

@[simp] lemma pos_zero : pos 0 = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma pos_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : pos n = 1 := by simp[pos, isLtNat, h]

def and (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 (n * m)

def or (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 (n + m)

lemma and_eq (n m : ℕ) : and n m = if 0 < n ∧ 0 < m then 1 else 0 := by simp [mul_pos_iff, and, isLtNat]

lemma and_eq_one (n m : ℕ) : and n m = 1 ↔ 0 < n ∧ 0 < m := by simp[and_eq, imp_false, Nat.pos_iff_ne_zero]

lemma or_eq (n m : ℕ) : or n m = if 0 < n ∨ 0 < m then 1 else 0 := by simp[or, isLtNat]

@[simp] lemma and_pos_iff (n m : ℕ) : 0 < and n m ↔ 0 < n ∧ 0 < m := by simp[and_eq]; by_cases 0 < n ∧ 0 < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma or_pos_iff (n m : ℕ) : 0 < or n m ↔ 0 < n ∨ 0 < m := by simp[or_eq]; by_cases 0 < n ∨ 0 < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma inv_pos_iff (n : ℕ) : 0 < inv n ↔ ¬0 < n := by simp[inv]

@[simp] lemma pos_pos_iff (n : ℕ) : 0 < pos n ↔ 0 < n := by simp[pos]

def ball (n : ℕ) (φ : ℕ → ℕ) : ℕ := n.rec 1 (fun n ih => (φ n).pos.and ih)

@[simp] lemma ball_pos_iff {φ : ℕ → ℕ} {n : ℕ} : 0 < ball n φ ↔ ∀ m < n, 0 < φ m := by
  induction' n with n ih <;> simp[ball, Nat.lt_succ_iff] at*
  · simp[ih]; exact ⟨
    by rintro ⟨hn, hp⟩ m hm; rcases lt_or_eq_of_le hm with (hm | rfl); { exact hp _ hm }; { exact hn },
    by intro h; exact ⟨h n (Nat.le_refl n), fun m hm => h m (le_of_lt hm)⟩⟩

@[simp] lemma ball_eq_zero_iff {φ : ℕ → ℕ} {n : ℕ} : ball n φ = 0 ↔ ∃ m < n, φ m = 0 := by
  simpa[-ball_pos_iff] using not_iff_not.mpr (ball_pos_iff (φ := φ) (n := n))

lemma ball_pos_iff_eq_one {φ : ℕ → ℕ} {n : ℕ} : ball n φ = 1 ↔ 0 < ball n φ := by
  induction' n with n _ <;> simp[ball, Nat.lt_succ_iff] at*
  · constructor
    · intro h; simpa using pos_of_eq_one h
    · intro h; simpa[and_eq_one] using h

inductive ArithPart₁ : ∀ {n}, (List.Vector ℕ n →. ℕ) → Prop
  | zero {n} : @ArithPart₁ n (fun _ => 0)
  | one {n} : @ArithPart₁ n (fun _ => 1)
  | add {n} (i j : Fin n) : @ArithPart₁ n (fun v => v.get i + v.get j : List.Vector ℕ n → ℕ)
  | mul {n} (i j : Fin n) : @ArithPart₁ n (fun v => v.get i * v.get j : List.Vector ℕ n → ℕ)
  | proj {n} (i : Fin n) : @ArithPart₁ n (fun v => v.get i : List.Vector ℕ n → ℕ)
  | equal {n} (i j : Fin n) : @ArithPart₁ n (fun v => isEqNat (v.get i) (v.get j) : List.Vector ℕ n → ℕ)
  | lt {n} (i j : Fin n) : @ArithPart₁ n (fun v => isLtNat (v.get i) (v.get j) : List.Vector ℕ n → ℕ)
  | comp {m n f} (g : Fin n → List.Vector ℕ m →. ℕ) :
    ArithPart₁ f → (∀ i, ArithPart₁ (g i)) → ArithPart₁ fun v => (List.Vector.mOfFn fun i => g i v) >>= f
  | rfind {n} {f : List.Vector ℕ (n + 1) → ℕ} :
    ArithPart₁ (n := n + 1) f → ArithPart₁ (fun v => rfind fun n => Part.some (f (n ::ᵥ v) = 0))

def Arith₁ (f : List.Vector ℕ n → ℕ) := by exact?

/--
`List.Vector α n` is the type of lists of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Note that there is also `Vector α n` in the root namespace,
which is the type of *arrays* of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Typically, if you are doing programming or verification, you will primarily use `Vector α n`,
and if you are doing mathematics, you may want to use `List.Vector α n` instead.
-/
def List.Vector (α : Type u) (n : ℕ) :=
  { l : List α // l.length = n }

informal_statement: If two vector functions are identical in value at every point, and one function belongs to the arithmetic progression class ArithPart₁, then the other function also belongs to the same class.
informal_proof: First, we recognize that the functions \( f \) and \( g \) are equal at every point by assumption. This means that for any input vector, both functions produce the same output. Since the property of belonging to the class ArithPart₁ is determined by the behavior of the function at each point, and \( f \) satisfies this property, it follows naturally that \( g \), which shares identical behavior everywhere, must also satisfy that property. Thus, \( g \) belongs to ArithPart₁ as well.

lemma pos_of_eq_one (h : n = 1) : 0 < n := by simp[h]

def isEqNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n = m then 1 else 0

def isLtNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n < m then 1 else 0

def isLeNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ≤ m then 1 else 0

def isDvdNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ∣ m then 1 else 0

@[simp] lemma isEqNat_pos_iff : 0 < isEqNat n m ↔ n = m := by simp[isEqNat]; by_cases n = m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLtNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLtNat n m ↔ n < m := by simp[isLtNat]; by_cases n < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLeNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLeNat n m ↔ n ≤ m := by simp[isLeNat]; by_cases n ≤ m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isDvdNat_pos_iff : 0 < isDvdNat n m ↔ n ∣ m := by simp[isDvdNat]; by_cases n ∣ m <;> simp[*]

def inv (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isEqNat n 0

def pos (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 n

@[simp] lemma inv_zero : inv 0 = 1 := rfl

@[simp] lemma inv_iff_ne_zero : inv n = 0 ↔ 0 < n := by simp[inv, isEqNat, zero_lt_iff]

@[simp] lemma inv_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : inv n = 0 := by simp[inv, isEqNat, h]

@[simp] lemma pos_zero : pos 0 = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma pos_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : pos n = 1 := by simp[pos, isLtNat, h]

def and (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 (n * m)

def or (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 (n + m)

lemma and_eq (n m : ℕ) : and n m = if 0 < n ∧ 0 < m then 1 else 0 := by simp [mul_pos_iff, and, isLtNat]

lemma and_eq_one (n m : ℕ) : and n m = 1 ↔ 0 < n ∧ 0 < m := by simp[and_eq, imp_false, Nat.pos_iff_ne_zero]

lemma or_eq (n m : ℕ) : or n m = if 0 < n ∨ 0 < m then 1 else 0 := by simp[or, isLtNat]

@[simp] lemma and_pos_iff (n m : ℕ) : 0 < and n m ↔ 0 < n ∧ 0 < m := by simp[and_eq]; by_cases 0 < n ∧ 0 < m <;> simp[*]

Note that there is also `Vector α n` in the root namespace,

informal_statement: Any arithmetic function $f$ that has the property specified by `ArithPart₁` also belongs to the class of functions defined by `Partrec'`.
informal_proof:
We will prove this by induction on the hypothesis `hf` of type `ArithPart₁ f`.

**Base Cases:**
1. **Case Zero:** When `f` is the constant function `0`, it trivially satisfies `Partrec'`.
2. **Case One:** Similarly, when `f` is the constant function `1`, it also trivially satisfies `Partrec'`.

**Inductive Step:**
We consider the inductive cases corresponding to each operation:

1. **Addition (`add`):** Suppose `f` is defined by addition. Since both operands of addition are known to satisfy `Partrec'`, their sum will also satisfy `Partrec'`. This follows from the closure properties of `Partrec'` under addition.

2. **Multiplication (`mul`):** If `f` is defined by multiplication, and both factors are known to satisfy `Partrec'`, then their product will also satisfy `Partrec'`. This is due to the closure of `Partrec'` under multiplication.

3. **Projection (`proj`):** For projection functions, which select specific components from a vector, the selected component trivially satisfies `Partrec'` as it is directly defined.

4. **Equality (`equal`):** Functions defined by equality (i.e., checking if two components are equal) naturally satisfy `Partrec'` because the condition directly relates to the values of those components.

5. **Less Than (`lt`):** Functions defined by comparing the magnitude of two components also satisfy `Partrec'`, as the comparison is a straightforward predicate over the values.

6. **Composition (`comp`):** If `f` is defined by composing two functions, and both are known to satisfy `Partrec'`, then the composition will also satisfy `Partrec'`. This relies on the closure of `Partrec'` under function composition.

7. **Recursion (`rfind`):** For functions defined recursively, each recursive step must satisfy `Partrec'`, and thus the entire function will satisfy `Partrec'`.

By systematically verifying each case and ensuring that the definition of `Partrec'` is closed under all these operations, we conclude that any `f` of type `ArithPart₁` is indeed of type `Partrec'`.

lemma pos_of_eq_one (h : n = 1) : 0 < n := by simp[h]

def isEqNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n = m then 1 else 0

def isLtNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n < m then 1 else 0

def isLeNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ≤ m then 1 else 0

def isDvdNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ∣ m then 1 else 0

@[simp] lemma isEqNat_pos_iff : 0 < isEqNat n m ↔ n = m := by simp[isEqNat]; by_cases n = m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLtNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLtNat n m ↔ n < m := by simp[isLtNat]; by_cases n < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLeNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLeNat n m ↔ n ≤ m := by simp[isLeNat]; by_cases n ≤ m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isDvdNat_pos_iff : 0 < isDvdNat n m ↔ n ∣ m := by simp[isDvdNat]; by_cases n ∣ m <;> simp[*]

def inv (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isEqNat n 0

def pos (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 n

@[simp] lemma inv_zero : inv 0 = 1 := rfl

@[simp] lemma inv_iff_ne_zero : inv n = 0 ↔ 0 < n := by simp[inv, isEqNat, zero_lt_iff]

@[simp] lemma inv_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : inv n = 0 := by simp[inv, isEqNat, h]

@[simp] lemma pos_zero : pos 0 = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma pos_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : pos n = 1 := by simp[pos, isLtNat, h]

def and (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 (n * m)

def or (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 (n + m)

lemma and_eq (n m : ℕ) : and n m = if 0 < n ∧ 0 < m then 1 else 0 := by simp [mul_pos_iff, and, isLtNat]

lemma and_eq_one (n m : ℕ) : and n m = 1 ↔ 0 < n ∧ 0 < m := by simp[and_eq, imp_false, Nat.pos_iff_ne_zero]

lemma or_eq (n m : ℕ) : or n m = if 0 < n ∨ 0 < m then 1 else 0 := by simp[or, isLtNat]

@[simp] lemma and_pos_iff (n m : ℕ) : 0 < and n m ↔ 0 < n ∧ 0 < m := by simp[and_eq]; by_cases 0 < n ∧ 0 < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma or_pos_iff (n m : ℕ) : 0 < or n m ↔ 0 < n ∨ 0 < m := by simp[or_eq]; by_cases 0 < n ∨ 0 < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma inv_pos_iff (n : ℕ) : 0 < inv n ↔ ¬0 < n := by simp[inv]

@[simp] lemma pos_pos_iff (n : ℕ) : 0 < pos n ↔ 0 < n := by simp[pos]

def ball (n : ℕ) (φ : ℕ → ℕ) : ℕ := n.rec 1 (fun n ih => (φ n).pos.and ih)

@[simp] lemma ball_pos_iff {φ : ℕ → ℕ} {n : ℕ} : 0 < ball n φ ↔ ∀ m < n, 0 < φ m := by

C1_dependencies.name: List.Vector
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`List.Vector α n` is the type of lists of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Note that there is also `Vector α n` in the root namespace,
which is the type of *arrays* of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Typically, if you are doing programming or verification, you will primarily use `Vector α n`,
and if you are doing mathematics, you may want to use `List.Vector α n` instead.
-/
def List.Vector (α : Type u) (n : ℕ) :=
  { l : List α // l.length = n }

/--
`List.Vector α n` is the type of lists of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Note that there is also `Vector α n` in the root namespace,
which is the type of *arrays* of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Typically, if you are doing programming or verification, you will primarily use `Vector α n`,
and if you are doing mathematics, you may want to use `List.Vector α n` instead.
-/
def List.Vector (α : Type u) (n : ℕ) :=
  { l : List α // l.length = n }

lemma pos_of_eq_one (h : n = 1) : 0 < n := by simp[h]

def isEqNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n = m then 1 else 0

def isLtNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n < m then 1 else 0

def isLeNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ≤ m then 1 else 0

def isDvdNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ∣ m then 1 else 0

@[simp] lemma isEqNat_pos_iff : 0 < isEqNat n m ↔ n = m := by simp[isEqNat]; by_cases n = m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLtNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLtNat n m ↔ n < m := by simp[isLtNat]; by_cases n < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLeNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLeNat n m ↔ n ≤ m := by simp[isLeNat]; by_cases n ≤ m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isDvdNat_pos_iff : 0 < isDvdNat n m ↔ n ∣ m := by simp[isDvdNat]; by_cases n ∣ m <;> simp[*]

def inv (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isEqNat n 0

def pos (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 n

@[simp] lemma inv_zero : inv 0 = 1 := rfl

@[simp] lemma inv_iff_ne_zero : inv n = 0 ↔ 0 < n := by simp[inv, isEqNat, zero_lt_iff]

@[simp] lemma inv_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : inv n = 0 := by simp[inv, isEqNat, h]

@[simp] lemma pos_zero : pos 0 = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma pos_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : pos n = 1 := by simp[pos, isLtNat, h]

def and (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 (n * m)

def or (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 (n + m)

lemma and_eq (n m : ℕ) : and n m = if 0 < n ∧ 0 < m then 1 else 0 := by simp [mul_pos_iff, and, isLtNat]

lemma and_eq_one (n m : ℕ) : and n m = 1 ↔ 0 < n ∧ 0 < m := by simp[and_eq, imp_false, Nat.pos_iff_ne_zero]

lemma or_eq (n m : ℕ) : or n m = if 0 < n ∨ 0 < m then 1 else 0 := by simp[or, isLtNat]

@[simp] lemma and_pos_iff (n m : ℕ) : 0 < and n m ↔ 0 < n ∧ 0 < m := by simp[and_eq]; by_cases 0 < n ∧ 0 < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma or_pos_iff (n m : ℕ) : 0 < or n m ↔ 0 < n ∨ 0 < m := by simp[or_eq]; by_cases 0 < n ∨ 0 < m <;> simp[*]

Note that there is also `Vector α n` in the root namespace,
which is the type of *arrays* of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Note that there is also `Vector α n` in the root namespace,
which is the type of *arrays* of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Typically, if you are doing programming or verification, you will primarily use `Vector α n`,
and if you are doing mathematics, you may want to use `List.Vector α n` instead.
-/
def List.Vector (α : Type u) (n : ℕ) :=
  { l : List α // l.length = n }

This construction satisfies the properties of associativity and the existence of an identity element, making it a commutative monoid under the component-wise multiplication operation.
informal_proof:
Let \( n \) be a natural number, and consider two vectors \( v \) and \( w \) of length \( n \), with components \( v_i \) and \( w_i \) respectively, where \( 0 \leq i < n \). The method `mul` takes these two vectors and returns a new vector \( u \) of length \( n \), where each component \( u_i \) is defined as the product of the corresponding components of \( v \) and \( w \), that is, \( u_i = v_i \times w_i \).

To show that `mul` is associative, let us consider three vectors \( v \), \( w \), and \( x \) of length \( n \). We want to verify that \( (v \cdot w) \cdot x = v \cdot (w \cdot x) \). Computing the \( i \)-th component of \( (v \cdot w) \cdot x \), we get:
\[
((v \cdot w) \cdot x)_i = (v \cdot w)_i \times x_i = (v_i \times w_i) \times x_i
\]
Similarly, the \( i \)-th component of \( v \cdot (w \cdot x) \) is:
\[
(v \cdot (w \cdot x))_i = v_i \times (w \cdot x)_i = v_i \times (w_i \times x_i)
\]
Since multiplication of natural numbers is associative, we have:
\[
(v_i \times w_i) \times x_i = v_i \times (w_i \times x_i)
\]
Thus, \( ((v \cdot w) \cdot x)_i = (v \cdot (w \cdot x))_i \) for all \( i \), which means \( (v \cdot w) \cdot x = v \cdot (w \cdot x) \).

Next, we need to establish the existence of an identity element. Consider the vector \( e \) where every component is 1, i.e., \( e_i = 1 \) for all \( i \). We claim that \( e \) is the identity element for the `mul` operation. To see this, take any vector \( v \) with components \( v_i \). Computing the \( i \)-th component of \( e \cdot v \), we have:
\[
(e \cdot v)_i = e_i \times v_i = 1 \times v_i = v_i
\]
Similarly,
\[
(v \cdot e)_i = v_i \times e_i = v_i \times 1 = v_i
\]
Therefore, \( e \cdot v = v \) and \( v \cdot e = v \) for all \( i \), showing that \( e \) indeed acts as the identity element for the `mul` operation.

C1_dependencies.name: List.Vector

/--
`List.Vector α n` is the type of lists of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Note that there is also `Vector α n` in the root namespace,
which is the type of *arrays* of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Typically, if you are doing programming or verification, you will primarily use `Vector α n`,
and if you are doing mathematics, you may want to use `List.Vector α n` instead.
-/
def List.Vector (α : Type u) (n : ℕ) :=
  { l : List α // l.length = n }

lemma pos_of_eq_one (h : n = 1) : 0 < n := by simp[h]

def isEqNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n = m then 1 else 0

def isLtNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n < m then 1 else 0

def isLeNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ≤ m then 1 else 0

def isDvdNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ∣ m then 1 else 0

@[simp] lemma isEqNat_pos_iff : 0 < isEqNat n m ↔ n = m := by simp[isEqNat]; by_cases n = m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLtNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLtNat n m ↔ n < m := by simp[isLtNat]; by_cases n < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLeNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLeNat n m ↔ n ≤ m := by simp[isLeNat]; by_cases n ≤ m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isDvdNat_pos_iff : 0 < isDvdNat n m ↔ n ∣ m := by simp[isDvdNat]; by_cases n ∣ m <;> simp[*]

def inv (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isEqNat n 0

def pos (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 n

@[simp] lemma inv_zero : inv 0 = 1 := rfl

@[simp] lemma inv_iff_ne_zero : inv n = 0 ↔ 0 < n := by simp[inv, isEqNat, zero_lt_iff]

@[simp] lemma inv_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : inv n = 0 := by simp[inv, isEqNat, h]

@[simp] lemma pos_zero : pos 0 = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma pos_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : pos n = 1 := by simp[pos, isLtNat, h]

def and (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 (n * m)

def or (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 (n + m)

lemma and_eq (n m : ℕ) : and n m = if 0 < n ∧ 0 < m then 1 else 0 := by simp [mul_pos_iff, and, isLtNat]

lemma and_eq_one (n m : ℕ) : and n m = 1 ↔ 0 < n ∧ 0 < m := by simp[and_eq, imp_false, Nat.pos_iff_ne_zero]

lemma or_eq (n m : ℕ) : or n m = if 0 < n ∨ 0 < m then 1 else 0 := by simp[or, isLtNat]

@[simp] lemma and_pos_iff (n m : ℕ) : 0 < and n m ↔ 0 < n ∧ 0 < m := by simp[and_eq]; by_cases 0 < n ∧ 0 < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma or_pos_iff (n m : ℕ) : 0 < or n m ↔ 0 < n ∨ 0 < m := by simp[or_eq]; by_cases 0 < n ∨ 0 < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma inv_pos_iff (n : ℕ) : 0 < inv n ↔ ¬0 < n := by simp[inv]

@[simp] lemma pos_pos_iff (n : ℕ) : 0 < pos n ↔ 0 < n := by simp[pos]

def ball (n : ℕ) (φ : ℕ → ℕ) : ℕ := n.rec 1 (fun n ih => (φ n).pos.and ih)

@[simp] lemma ball_pos_iff {φ : ℕ → ℕ} {n : ℕ} : 0 < ball n φ ↔ ∀ m < n, 0 < φ m := by
  induction' n with n ih <;> simp[ball, Nat.lt_succ_iff] at*

informal_statement: For a vector of length $n$ over the natural numbers, two elements at positions $i$ and $j$ are equal if and only if $i$ and $j$ are the same position within that vector.
informal_proof:
Let us consider a vector `v` of length `n` with elements indexed by `Fin n`, which represents the positions from `0` to `n-1`.

1. **If** `i` equals `j`, **then** the elements `v.get i` and `v.get j` must be the same because they refer to the same position in the vector.
2. **Conversely**, if `v.get i` equals `v.get j`, **then** `i` must equal `j` because, in a well-defined vector, different positions hold distinct (or at least individually identified) elements. 

This bidirectional implication confirms that the equality of elements in the vector is strictly determined by the equality of their indices within that vector.

lemma pos_of_eq_one (h : n = 1) : 0 < n := by simp[h]

def isEqNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n = m then 1 else 0

def isLtNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n < m then 1 else 0

def isLeNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ≤ m then 1 else 0

def isDvdNat (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := if n ∣ m then 1 else 0

@[simp] lemma isEqNat_pos_iff : 0 < isEqNat n m ↔ n = m := by simp[isEqNat]; by_cases n = m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLtNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLtNat n m ↔ n < m := by simp[isLtNat]; by_cases n < m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isLeNat_pos_iff : 0 < isLeNat n m ↔ n ≤ m := by simp[isLeNat]; by_cases n ≤ m <;> simp[*]

@[simp] lemma isDvdNat_pos_iff : 0 < isDvdNat n m ↔ n ∣ m := by simp[isDvdNat]; by_cases n ∣ m <;> simp[*]

def inv (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isEqNat n 0

def pos (n : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 n

@[simp] lemma inv_zero : inv 0 = 1 := rfl

@[simp] lemma inv_iff_ne_zero : inv n = 0 ↔ 0 < n := by simp[inv, isEqNat, zero_lt_iff]

@[simp] lemma inv_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : inv n = 0 := by simp[inv, isEqNat, h]

@[simp] lemma pos_zero : pos 0 = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma pos_ne_zero (h : n ≠ 0) : pos n = 1 := by simp[pos, isLtNat, h]

def and (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 (n * m)

def or (n m : ℕ) : ℕ := isLtNat 0 (n + m)

lemma and_eq (n m : ℕ) : and n m = if 0 < n ∧ 0 < m then 1 else 0 := by simp [mul_pos_iff, and, isLtNat]

Note that there is also `Vector α n` in the root namespace,

C1_dependencies.name: List.Vector

/--
`List.Vector α n` is the type of lists of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Note that there is also `Vector α n` in the root namespace,
which is the type of *arrays* of length `n` with elements of type `α`.

Typically, if you are doing programming or verification, you will primarily use `Vector α n`,
and if you are doing mathematics, you may want to use `List.Vector α n` instead.
-/
def List.Vector (α : Type u) (n : ℕ) :=
  { l : List α // l.length = n }

For any natural number \( n \) and function \( \phi: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \), the \( \phi \)-ball centered at \( n \) being equal to 1 is equivalent to the condition where \( \phi(n) \) is greater than 0.

**Forward Direction:** Suppose the \( \phi \)-ball around \( n \) is equal to 1. By the definition of the \( \phi \)-ball, this means that \( \phi(n) \) is exactly 1. Since 1 is certainly greater than 0, it follows that \( \phi(n) \) is positive.

**Reverse Direction:** Conversely, assume that \( \phi(n) \) is greater than 0. This implies that \( \phi(n) \) must be at least 1, as it is a natural number. Given that the \( \phi \)-ball around \( n \) is defined to be equal to 1 precisely when \( \phi(n) \) is exactly 1, it follows that the \( \phi \)-ball is equal to 1.

Through these two implications, we conclude that the \( \phi \)-ball centered at \( n \) being equal to 1 is indeed equivalent to \( \phi(n) \) being greater than 0.

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

4. **Conclusion**: Combining both directions, we conclude that \( \text{pos}(n) > 0 \) precisely when \( n > 0 \).

informal_statement: For any two natural numbers \( n \) and \( m \), the logical conjunction \( n \land m \) equals 1 if and only if both \( n \) and \( m \) are greater than 0.
informal_proof:
First, we recognize that in the context of natural numbers, a "logical conjunction" \( n \land m \) being equal to 1 implies that both \( n \) and \( m \) are non-zero. This is because, in many mathematical frameworks, especially within the natural numbers starting from 0, a value of 1 represents truth (i.e., the absence of zero). 

We then apply the equivalence between a natural number being positive and it not being equal to zero, captured by the lemma `Nat.pos_iff_ne_zero`. This tells us that \( n > 0 \) and \( m > 0 \) are equivalent to \( n \neq 0 \) and \( m \neq 0 \), respectively.

The simplification step in the Lean4 proof leverages the definition of logical conjunction in terms of negations, where \( n \land m \) is equivalent to \( \neg (n = 0 \lor m = 0) \). This means that \( n \land m \) being 1 is equivalent to neither \( n \) nor \( m \) being 0, which directly translates to both \( n \) and \( m \) being greater than 0.

Conversely, if both \( n \) and \( m \) are greater than 0, they cannot be 0, so their conjunction \( n \land m \) naturally evaluates to 1. This completes the proof that \( n \land m = 1 \) holds precisely when both \( n \) and \( m \) are greater than 0.

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/

informal_proof: Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that there are only finitely many primes, say \( p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k \), and that all these primes are \( \leq n \) for some natural number \( n \). Consider the number \( m = (n+1)! + 1 \). Since \( m \) is greater than all the primes \( p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k \), none of these primes can divide \( m \) without leaving a remainder of 1. However, any prime dividing \( m \) must be greater than \( n \), which contradicts our initial assumption that all primes \( \leq n \) are \( p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k \). Therefore, our assumption is false, and there must exist a prime \( p > n \) for any given natural number \( n \). This proves that there are infinitely many primes.

informal_statement: There are infinitely many prime numbers.
informal_proof:
To prove that there are infinitely many prime numbers, we proceed by contradiction.

First, we take an arbitrary natural number \( n \).

Next, we consider the number \( (n + 1)! + 1 \), where \( ! \) denotes the factorial operation. By the definition of factorial, \( (n + 1)! \) is the product of all positive integers up to \( n + 1 \). Adding 1 to this product results in \( (n + 1)! + 1 \), which is at least 2, as factorial grows rapidly.

We then assert that any number greater than 1 has at least one prime factor. Therefore, \( (n + 1)! + 1 \) must have a prime factor \( p \).

We aim to demonstrate that this prime factor \( p \) is greater than \( n \). Suppose, for contradiction, that \( p \) is not greater than \( n \). If \( p \) is a prime number less than or equal to \( n \), then \( p \) divides \( (n + 1)! \) because factorial includes all numbers up to \( n + 1 \).

Since \( p \) divides both \( (n + 1)! \) and \( (n + 1)! + 1 \), it must also divide their difference:
\[
(n + 1)! + 1 - (n + 1)! = 1
\]
This implies \( p \) divides 1, which is impossible because the only positive integer that divides 1 is 1 itself, and primes are greater than 1.

This contradiction establishes that our initial assumption is false. Therefore, the prime factor \( p \) must be greater than \( n \).

Since \( n \) was arbitrary, this argument applies to any natural number. Hence, there is no largest prime number, and thus, there are infinitely many primes.
